title: Flutter state: Provider and Bloc
tagline: Who holds the value, and who rebuilds when it changes.
intro: Both packages solve the same two problems: reading a value from anywhere in the tree, and rebuilding only the widgets that care. The difference is how much structure they ask for in return.

sections.title: What state management is for
sections.summary: Not storing values — deciding who rebuilds when one changes.

body: setState already stores state perfectly well. What it cannot do is share a value with a screen three routes away, or rebuild one widget instead of a whole subtree. Every package here exists for those two problems.

blocks.caption: The same tap, with and without something listening.

items.label: setState in a StatefulWidget
items.detail: Marks this element dirty, so build() runs again for it and for everything below it
explain: setState is not slow, it is coarse: the whole subtree under that widget is rebuilt, however small the value that changed was.
For a checkbox or an expanded card that is exactly right, and reaching for a package there is more machinery than the problem deserves.
const constructors are what limit the damage: an identical const widget is reused rather than rebuilt, so the cost stops at the first non-const node.

items.label: Then a second screen needs it
items.detail: The same value has to be read somewhere else, and passing it down six constructors starts to hurt
explain: Passing a value through widgets that do not use it is prop drilling, and every one of those constructors has to change when the value does.
Lifting the state to a common ancestor solves the reading, and makes the rebuilding worse: now the ancestor rebuilds, so both branches do.
The real requirement is two things at once — read it from anywhere, and rebuild only the widgets that care.

items.label: InheritedWidget underneath
items.detail: Flutter's own answer: read a value from an ancestor in constant time, and be told when it changes
explain: Theme.of(context) and MediaQuery.of(context) are this mechanism. Provider, Riverpod and Bloc are all wrappers over the same thing.
The lookup is O(1): each element keeps a map of inherited widgets by type, so walking the tree is not part of the cost.
Calling .of(context) registers this element as a dependent, and that registration is what makes the next step possible.

items.label: The widget subscribes
items.detail: Reading through context registers a dependency, so this widget alone is scheduled when the value changes
explain: context.watch in Provider and BlocBuilder in Bloc both come down to this registration — the API differs, the mechanism does not.
The subscription is per element, so two widgets reading the same object are notified independently of each other.

items.label: One widget rebuilds
items.detail: Its parents do not, its siblings do not, and the rest of the frame costs nothing
explain: This is the whole win: the same value change costs one build method instead of a subtree of them.
It also explains why 'my whole screen rebuilds' is almost always a subscription placed too high, not a slow framework.

items.label: And the state outlives the build
items.detail: It lives in an object above the widget, so a rebuild — or a route change — does not lose it
explain: A StatefulWidget's State survives rebuilds but not the route being popped, and it is invisible to any other screen.
Moving the value into a notifier or a bloc held above the route is what makes it survivable and shareable at the same time.

items: Ask two questions: who else reads this, and how much of the screen may rebuild when it changes.
If the answers are 'nobody' and 'this widget', setState is the right answer and needs no defending.
Everything below is the same idea with different ergonomics: a value above the tree, and a subscription per widget.

sections.title: Provider and ChangeNotifier
sections.summary: The smallest step up from setState, and the three ways to read.

blocks.caption: Adding an item to the cart, and who hears about it.

items.label: ChangeNotifier
items.detail: A plain Dart class with a list of listeners and one method to call when something changed
explain: It is not magic: mixin ChangeNotifier gives you addListener, removeListener and notifyListeners, and nothing else.
Your model owns the data and the methods that change it, so the widget layer never mutates a field directly.
Expose the list as unmodifiable. A caller that can add to it directly can change state without anyone being notified.

items.label: ChangeNotifierProvider
items.detail: Creates the notifier above the tree, hands it down through context, and disposes it on removal
explain: Use create: to build it, never a value: with a newly constructed object — a rebuild of the parent would silently make a second one.
Disposal is handled for you, which is the main reason to use the package instead of an InheritedWidget you wrote yourself.
MultiProvider is the same thing for several models, and it keeps the tree from turning into a staircase of nested providers.

items.label: context.watch<CartModel>()
items.detail: Read the model and subscribe: this widget rebuilds on every notifyListeners()
explain: Every call to notifyListeners rebuilds every watcher, whatever changed — that is the coarse edge of Provider.
So watch as low in the tree as you can. A watch in the screen's build method is the usual reason a whole page rebuilds.

items.label: context.read<CartModel>()
items.detail: Read once without subscribing — what you call inside onPressed and other callbacks
explain: Using watch inside a callback subscribes the widget for no reason; using read inside build gives you a stale value on the next change.
The rule of thumb: read in callbacks, watch in build, and let the analyzer's provider lint catch the ones you get backwards.

items.label: context.select
items.detail: Subscribe to one derived value, and rebuild only when that value changes
explain: select<CartModel, int>((c) => c.items.length) rebuilds when the count changes, and not when an item's title is edited.
It compares with ==, so the value you select must be something comparable — an int, a String, a value object, not a fresh List each time.
This is the fix for 'everything rebuilds' that does not require restructuring the widget tree.

items.label: Consumer<CartModel>
items.detail: Narrow the rebuild to a builder, and pass the expensive part in as a child that is never rebuilt
explain: Consumer's builder receives a child argument: whatever you pass there is built once and reused on every rebuild.
It exists for the case where you cannot move the subscription down, because the widget that needs the value is deep inside a const-heavy tree.

blocks.caption: The whole of Provider in one screen: a model that notifies, a provider that owns it, and a select that narrows the rebuild.

body: notifyListeners() is all-or-nothing: it wakes every watcher of that model. A model that holds the whole screen's state will rebuild the whole screen — split the model, or use select.

sections.title: Bloc and Cubit
sections.summary: Events in, states out, and nothing mutated on the way through.

blocks.caption: Pull to refresh, as an event and the states it produces.

items.label: The widget adds an event
items.detail: context.read<ProfileBloc>().add(ProfileRefreshed()) — a value naming what happened, not what to do
explain: An event is a class, so it is comparable, loggable and replayable: the whole history of a screen is a list of these objects.
The widget never calls the repository and never decides anything. It reports the gesture and waits for a state.
Use read here, not watch — adding an event is a callback, and subscribing in a callback is the classic mistake.

items.label: on<Event> handles it
items.detail: The registered handler runs, calls whatever it needs, and emits states as it goes
explain: Handlers are async, and events are processed one at a time by default, so two taps cannot interleave halfway through.
Transformers change that when you need it: droppable() ignores taps while one is in flight, restartable() cancels the previous.
This is where the screen's logic lives, and it is testable with no widgets at all — feed events in, assert the states that come out.

items.label: emit(ProfileLoading())
items.detail: Each emit pushes an immutable state onto the stream; nothing is mutated in place
explain: States are separate classes or a sealed hierarchy, so 'loading with old data' and 'loaded' cannot quietly be true at once.
Bloc drops an emit equal to the current state, which is why states need == — Equatable or a data-class-like override.
Emitting after the handler completes throws. If work continues past the handler, it belongs in a stream the bloc listens to.

items.label: BlocBuilder rebuilds
items.detail: The widget under it rebuilds once per state, and buildWhen filters the states it should ignore
explain: BlocBuilder subscribes to the stream and nothing above it rebuilds — the same narrow subscription Provider gets from select.
BlocSelector is the finer version: rebuild only when one field of the state changes, for the same reason select exists.

items.label: BlocListener for one-off effects
items.detail: Snackbars, navigation, dialogs — things that must happen once per state, not once per build
explain: A build method can run many times for the same state, so showing a snackbar there gives you three snackbars.
BlocConsumer is the two combined when a widget genuinely needs to rebuild and to fire an effect from the same state.

items.label: Cubit, when events are ceremony
items.detail: The same states and the same stream, but with methods instead of an event class per action
explain: cubit.refresh() calls emit directly. You lose the recorded event objects and the transformers, and you keep everything else.
Start with Cubit and move to Bloc when you need the event log, debouncing, or a handler that has to cancel the previous one.

blocks.caption: A sealed state hierarchy and one handler — the shape a bloc keeps however big the screen gets.

items: One bloc per screen or per feature, not one per app: a bloc that knows everything is a ViewModel with extra steps.
bloc_test drives the whole thing without a widget tree — act, then assert the exact list of emitted states.
BlocProvider owns the lifetime, and closes the bloc when the route goes.

sections.title: Which one to reach for
sections.summary: Four answers, and the question that separates them.

rows: A second set of concepts to learn

items: Does only this widget read it? Use setState and stop.
Does another screen read it, and is the logic thin? Provider with select is enough.
Is the screen a sequence of states you would draw on a whiteboard? That is a bloc, and the events are already named.
Is the value derived from other values, or scoped per item? Riverpod's providers do that without a widget in the tree.

body: Mixing them is normal and not a failure: a bloc for the checkout flow, a Provider for the cart, setState for a dropdown on one screen. What is not normal is two packages owning the same value.

sections.title: Where it goes wrong
sections.summary: The four bugs every Flutter codebase writes at least once.

blocks.caption: A rebuild storm, and where to cut it.

items.label: One model holds the screen
items.detail: Every field of the page lives in a single ChangeNotifier, and every change calls notifyListeners()
explain: Editing a search box then notifies the list, the header, the filter chips and the footer — none of which read that field.
The fix is either smaller models, one per concern, or select so each widget subscribes to the value it actually uses.

items.label: The subscription sits too high
items.detail: context.watch in the screen's build method, so the whole page rebuilds for any change at all
explain: Every widget below is rebuilt because its parent was, and the const constructors that would have stopped it are usually missing too.
Move the watch down to the widget that displays the value, even if that means extracting a small widget to hold it.

items.label: BuildContext across an async gap
items.detail: await, then use context — by then the widget may be gone and the Navigator call throws
explain: The analyzer's use_build_context_synchronously lint flags it, and the fix is to check mounted after every await before touching context.
Capture what you need before the await instead: a Navigator or a ScaffoldMessenger taken beforehand does not need the context afterwards.

items.label: Effects in build
items.detail: Showing a snackbar, navigating or firing analytics from a build method that runs many times
explain: Build must be free of side effects, because Flutter may call it again for reasons that have nothing to do with your state.
BlocListener, or a one-shot flag in the state, is where those belong — anything that must happen once per event rather than once per frame.

items.label: Nothing is disposed
items.detail: A controller, a stream subscription or a timer created in the widget and never cancelled
explain: Providers dispose the objects they create; anything you construct yourself in initState you have to cancel in dispose.
The symptom is a callback firing after the screen is gone, usually surfacing as a setState on an unmounted widget.

rows: watch at the top of build
